title: Abbey and Trappist Beer Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: The difference between Trappist and abbey beer, what the Authentic Trappist Product label means and the styles to know.
teaser: Every Trappist beer is brewed in a monastery. Most abbey beers are not. Here is how to tell them apart.
standfirst: Trappist and abbey beers are often confused, but the words mean different things. One is a protected label tied to working monasteries. The other is a broad family of Belgian-style beers. Here is the difference and the styles worth knowing.
sections: Trappist is a label with rules

Trappists are a Catholic order of monks and nuns, formally the Order of Cistercians of the Strict Observance. Several Trappist monasteries brew beer to support themselves. In 1997 a group of these monasteries formed the International Trappist Association to protect the name and created the Authentic Trappist Product logo.

To carry that logo, a beer must be made within the walls of a Trappist monastery, by the monks or under their supervision. The brewery must be secondary to monastic life. Income must support the community, with any surplus given to charity. The number of breweries holding the label changes from time to time as monasteries open, close or step back.
Abbey beer is a broader idea

Abbey beer is a looser term. It usually means a beer brewed in the monastic Belgian tradition, often by a commercial brewery. Some abbey beers are brewed under licence from an existing or former abbey, which receives a royalty. Others simply borrow the style and the imagery.

In Belgium a separate logo, Certified Belgian Abbey Beer, marks beers linked to a real abbey. Outside Belgium the word abbey on a label tells you only that the brewer is working in that tradition. It does not mean a monk has been anywhere near the tank.

That distinction matters when you are buying. An authentic Trappist beer from Belgium will cost more in India once import duty and shipping are added. An abbey-style beer from a local brewery may be excellent in its own right. Judge it on what is in the glass, not on the picture of a monastery on the label.

Among the Belgian Trappist breweries, a few names come up again and again. Westmalle is closely associated with the dubbel and tripel styles that so many breweries now imitate. Chimay is one of the most widely exported. Rochefort is known for strong dark beers. Orval makes one main beer, dry hopped and conditioned with Brettanomyces yeast. Westvleteren sells its beer in limited quantities, mainly from the abbey itself.

These breweries do not all make the same styles. What they share is the label, the monastic setting and a reputation built over generations.

Belgian monastic beers fall into a loose ladder of strength. The single or patersbier, originally brewed for the monks themselves, is pale and modest, around 4.8 to 6% ABV. The dubbel is dark amber to brown, malty and fruity, around 6 to 7.6%. The tripel is pale gold and strong, around 7.5 to 9.5%, dry and spicy. Stronger dark beers, often called quadrupel, can exceed 10%.

Our guides to the Belgian dubbel, the Belgian tripel and dubbel versus quadrupel explain each in more detail.
The yeast and sugar behind the flavour

Belgian monastic beers get much of their character from yeast. These strains produce fruity esters, such as pear, banana and plum. They also make spicy phenols that smell of clove or pepper. Fermentation often runs warm, sometimes rising into the mid twenties Celsius, which brings out those flavours.

Brewers also add sugar, often as candi sugar or syrup. That sounds odd for a strong beer, but sugar ferments completely. It raises alcohol while keeping the body light and the finish dry. Many of these beers are bottle conditioned, refermented with a small dose of sugar and yeast in the bottle for lively carbonation.
Strong beers in a warm climate

Tripels and quadrupels can be 8 to 11% ABV while drinking deceptively easily. In Indian heat that is a trap. Serve them in a small chalice or tulip at around 8 to 12 °C, sip slowly, drink water alongside and never drive afterwards.

They also need careful storage. Bottle conditioned beers carry live yeast and change with time. Heat speeds up that change. An imported bottle that has spent weeks in a hot warehouse can arrive flat, oxidised or with yeast flavours gone stale. Buy from importers who keep stock cool.

Food is where these beers shine. A dubbel suits slow-cooked meats, roasted root vegetables or a Kolkata-style mutton biryani. A tripel cuts through rich, buttery dishes such as a chicken makhani. A Trappist single works with lighter fare, from grilled fish to a plate of paneer tikka. Pour a little less than you think and let the beer warm slightly as you eat.

Belgian monastic beers are a masterclass in yeast-driven flavour. Learning to tell banana from pear, clove from pepper or a pleasant warmth from hot solvent alcohol takes practice with reference samples and guidance. Those skills carry across every style you will ever taste.

For a first step, pour a dubbel and a tripel side by side. Note the colour, then the aroma. Try to name one fruit and one spice in each. You will start to hear the yeast talking.
faqs: What is the difference between Trappist and abbey beer?

Trappist beer is brewed inside a Trappist monastery under the monks' supervision and can carry the Authentic Trappist Product logo. Abbey beer is a broader term for beers in the monastic tradition, often from commercial breweries.
Do monks really brew Trappist beer?
Trappist beer must be brewed within the monastery walls by the monks or under their supervision, though lay staff often do much of the work.
What are the main Trappist styles?
The main family runs from the light single to the dubbel, the tripel and strong dark beers often called quadrupel.
Why do Belgian abbey beers use sugar?
Sugar ferments completely, raising alcohol while keeping the body light and the finish dry.
